title: Human Reproduction
description: Grade 12 Biology: the male and female reproductive systems, gametogenesis and the menstrual cycle, and fertilisation, pregnancy and embryonic development.

topics.title: The Male and Female Reproductive Systems
topics.concept:
Humans reproduce sexually: a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg/ovum) fuse to form a new individual. The body has specialised reproductive systems for making gametes and supporting the developing baby.

The male reproductive system consists of:

  • A pair of testes — held in a sac (the scrotum) outside the body, where it is slightly cooler; the testes make sperm and the male hormone testosterone.
  • Ducts — the epididymis, vas deferens and urethra — that store and carry the sperm.
  • Glands (such as the prostate and seminal vesicles) that add fluid to make semen.
  • The penis, which delivers the sperm.

The female reproductive system consists of:

  • A pair of ovaries — which make the eggs (ova) and the female hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
  • A pair of oviducts (fallopian tubes) — which carry the egg from the ovary toward the uterus; fertilisation usually happens here.
  • The uterus (womb) — a muscular organ where the baby develops.
  • The vagina — which receives the sperm and is the birth canal.

So the male system is built to produce and deliver sperm, while the female system produces eggs and nurtures the growing baby.

examples.problem: Example 1: Where are sperm produced, and why are the testes located outside the body?
examples.solution:
The testes are in the scrotum.

  • Sperm are produced in the testes.
  • They lie outside (in the scrotum) where it is slightly cooler, which sperm production needs.
examples.answer: Sperm are produced in the testes, which lie in the scrotum outside the body because sperm formation needs a slightly cooler temperature.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the function of the ovaries?
examples.solution:
The ovaries are the female gonads.

  • They make the eggs (ova).
  • They make the female hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
examples.answer: The ovaries produce the eggs (ova) and the female hormones oestrogen and progesterone.

examples.problem: Example 3: Where does fertilisation usually take place, and where does the baby develop?
examples.solution:
Different organs do different jobs.

  • Fertilisation usually occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
  • The baby develops in the uterus.
examples.answer: Fertilisation usually occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube); the baby develops in the uterus.

recap:
• Male: testes (in scrotum — sperm + testosterone) → ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, urethra) + glands → semen; delivered by the penis.
  • Female: ovaries (eggs + oestrogen/progesterone), oviducts (fertilisation site), uterus (baby develops), vagina (birth canal).

quiz.q: Sperm and testosterone are produced by the:
quiz.explanation: The testes make sperm and the hormone testosterone.

quiz.q: Fertilisation in humans usually takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: Fertilisation usually happens in the oviduct.

topics.title: Gametogenesis and the Menstrual Cycle
topics.concept:
The formation of gametes is called gametogenesis. The making of sperm is spermatogenesis and the making of eggs is oogenesis; both involve meiosis, so the gametes are haploid (half the chromosome number).

  • Spermatogenesis happens in the testes and produces large numbers of tiny, motile sperm continuously from puberty onward. A sperm has a head (with the nucleus), a middle piece (with mitochondria for energy) and a tail (for swimming).
  • Oogenesis happens in the ovaries and produces eggs. Usually only one egg is released about once a month; the release of the egg from the ovary is called ovulation.

In females, the reproductive events repeat in a roughly 28-day cycle called the menstrual cycle, controlled by hormones. Its main phases are:

  • Menstrual phase (about days 1–5) — if no fertilisation has happened, the thickened lining of the uterus breaks down and is shed as the menstrual flow.
  • Follicular/proliferative phase — an egg matures in the ovary and the uterus lining thickens again.
  • Ovulation (around day 14) — the mature egg is released.
  • Luteal/secretory phase — the uterus is prepared to receive a fertilised egg; if none arrives, the cycle repeats.

The menstrual cycle begins at puberty (menarche) and stops around middle age (menopause).

examples.problem: Example 1: What is gametogenesis, and why does it involve meiosis?
examples.solution:
Gametes must be haploid.

  • Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes (sperm and eggs).
  • It involves meiosis so the gametes are haploid, restoring the normal number at fertilisation.
examples.answer: Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes; it uses meiosis so the gametes are haploid.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is ovulation, and roughly when does it occur in a 28-day cycle?
examples.solution:
Ovulation is the egg's release.

  • Ovulation is the release of the mature egg from the ovary.
  • It occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.
examples.answer: Ovulation is the release of the mature egg from the ovary, around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.

examples.problem: Example 3: What happens during the menstrual phase?
examples.solution:
It occurs when there is no fertilisation.

  • The thickened lining of the uterus breaks down.
  • It is shed as the menstrual flow (about days 1-5).
examples.answer: If no fertilisation occurs, the thickened uterine lining breaks down and is shed as the menstrual flow.

recap:
• Gametogenesis (meiosis → haploid gametes): spermatogenesis (testes; many sperm: head/middle/tail) and oogenesis (ovaries; one egg/month).
  • Ovulation = release of the egg (~day 14).
  • Menstrual cycle (~28 days): menstrual → follicular → ovulation → luteal.
  • Starts at menarche (puberty), ends at menopause.

quiz.q: The release of a mature egg from the ovary is called:
quiz.explanation: Ovulation is the release of the egg, around day 14.

quiz.q: Gametes are haploid because gametogenesis involves:
quiz.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, making haploid gametes.

topics.title: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Development
topics.concept:
When sperm are deposited in the female tract, they swim toward the egg in the oviduct. Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm with the egg to form a single cell, the zygote, which is diploid and carries genes from both parents. Only one sperm normally enters the egg.

The zygote begins to divide by mitosis as it travels down the oviduct, becoming a ball of cells called the blastocyst (embryo). About a week after fertilisation, this embryo embeds itself in the thick, prepared lining of the uterus — a step called implantation. This marks the start of pregnancy (gestation).

After implantation, a special structure called the placenta develops, connecting the embryo to the wall of the uterus through the umbilical cord. The placenta is the lifeline of the baby: it allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from the mother's blood to the baby, and carbon dioxide and wastes to pass back to be removed by the mother. It also makes hormones that maintain the pregnancy.

Over about nine months, the embryo (later called a foetus) grows and all its organs form and mature. The major organs begin to form in the first three months. Finally, the muscular uterus contracts strongly in the process of childbirth (parturition), and the baby is born. After birth the mother's mammary glands produce milk (lactation) to feed the baby; the first milk (colostrum) is rich in antibodies that protect the newborn.

Right after fertilisation, the zygote begins repeated mitotic divisions called cleavage as it moves down the oviduct. These divisions first form a solid ball of cells called the morula, which then develops a cavity to become the hollow blastocyst — the stage that implants in the uterine wall.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is fertilisation, and what is the cell formed called?
examples.solution:
Two gametes fuse.

  • Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm with the egg.
  • It forms a diploid cell called the zygote.
examples.answer: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm and an egg to form the zygote.

examples.solution:
It happens about a week after fertilisation.

  • The early embryo (blastocyst) embeds in the prepared lining of the uterus.
  • This starts pregnancy.
examples.answer: Implantation is the embedding of the early embryo into the uterine lining, which begins pregnancy.

examples.problem: Example 3: State two functions of the placenta.
examples.solution:
The placenta links the baby to the mother.

  • It supplies oxygen and nutrients from mother to baby.
  • It removes CO₂ and wastes from the baby (and makes hormones).
examples.answer: The placenta supplies the baby with oxygen and nutrients and removes its CO₂ and wastes (and makes hormones that maintain pregnancy).

recap:
• Fertilisation (in oviduct): sperm + egg → diploid zygote.
  • Zygote divides → blastocyst; implantation in uterus lining → pregnancy.
  • Placenta (via umbilical cord): supplies O₂/nutrients, removes CO₂/wastes, makes hormones.
  • ~9 months gestation → childbirth (parturition); then lactation (colostrum rich in antibodies).
  • Early development: zygote → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → implantation.

quiz.q: The diploid cell formed by the fusion of sperm and egg is the:
The structure that supplies the baby with oxygen and nutrients in the womb is the:
quiz.explanation: The placenta exchanges materials between mother and baby.

questions.q: The male gamete in humans is the:
questions.explanation: The sperm is the male gamete.

questions.q: Sperm are produced in the:
questions.explanation: The testes produce sperm.

questions.q: The testes lie outside the body in the scrotum because sperm formation needs:
questions.explanation: Sperm production requires a temperature slightly below body temperature.

questions.q: Eggs and female hormones are produced by the:
questions.explanation: The ovaries make eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.q: The organ in which the baby develops is the:
questions.explanation: The baby develops in the uterus (womb).

questions.q: Formation of gametes is called:
questions.explanation: Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes.

questions.q: The making of sperm is called:
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis is sperm formation in the testes.

questions.q: Gametes are haploid because gametogenesis involves:
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number.

questions.q: Release of a mature egg from the ovary is called:
questions.explanation: Ovulation is the release of the egg, around day 14.

questions.q: A typical menstrual cycle lasts about:
questions.explanation: The menstrual cycle is about 28 days long.

questions.q: Fusion of a sperm and egg is called:
questions.explanation: Fertilisation is the fusion of the gametes.

questions.q: Fertilisation usually occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Fertilisation normally takes place in the oviduct.

questions.q: Embedding of the early embryo in the uterine lining is:
questions.explanation: Implantation begins pregnancy.

questions.q: The structure that supplies the baby with oxygen and nutrients is the:
questions.explanation: The placenta exchanges materials between mother and baby.

questions.q: Human gestation (pregnancy) lasts about:
questions.explanation: Human pregnancy lasts about nine months.

questions.q: A sperm's middle piece is packed with mitochondria because it must:
options: Provide energy for the tail to swim
questions.explanation: Mitochondria supply the ATP needed to power the sperm's tail movement toward the egg.

questions.q: If fertilisation does NOT occur in a cycle, the thickened uterine lining is:
questions.explanation: Without a fertilised egg to implant, the lining breaks down and is shed during menstruation.

questions.q: The zygote is diploid even though the gametes are haploid because fertilisation:
options: Combines the chromosomes of both gametes
questions.explanation: Joining two haploid sets restores the full diploid chromosome number in the zygote.

questions.q: The placenta is described as the baby's lifeline because it carries out exchange of:
options: Nutrients, oxygen and wastes between mother and baby
questions.explanation: Across the placenta the baby gains O₂ and nutrients and gives up CO₂ and wastes.

questions.q: Colostrum, the first breast milk, is especially valuable to a newborn because it is rich in:
questions.explanation: Colostrum supplies antibodies that give the newborn early immunity.

questions.q: Only one sperm normally fertilises an egg; mechanisms blocking extra sperm prevent the zygote from becoming:
questions.explanation: Allowing several sperm would give an extra set of chromosomes, producing an abnormal, non-viable zygote.
